sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 2022. Comprehensive Bibliography of Chadic and Hausa Linguistics, 5th edition. IUScholarWorks.
sources.note: Used to enumerate every Kanakuru-keyed work (Newman 1970/1972a/1972b/1974/1979h/2006b/2013, Schuh 1972/1974a/1974e, Leben 1974, Frajzyngier 1976, Churma 1982, Hudson 1984, Johnson 1989, Tuller 1992b, Samek-Lodovici 1998, Zoll 2003, Kidda Awak 2005, Lax 1986, Jungraithmayr 1972b, Wolff 1954/1959, Meek 1931, Migeod 1924, Kraft 1981). No work on Kanakuru stress or accent is listed.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page dera1248 and WALS languoid knk
sources.note: Glottolog Glottolog's most extensive descriptions: Newman 1974 (grammar), Newman 1971 (grammar), Meek 1931 (wordlist). WALS source for Kanakuru is Newman 1974 (no stress feature values shown).

sources.citation: Downing, Laura J. 2025. Testing typologies of laryngeal markedness on African languages. Studies in African Linguistics 54.
sources.note: Kanakuru row (citing Maddieson 1984 / Newman 1974, Wolff 1959) covers stop laryngeal types only; nothing on stress.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 2013. Study Hausa, understand Kanakuru. In Ndimele et al. (eds.), Language, Literature and Culture in a Multilingual Society: A Festschrift for Abubakar Rasheed, 221-230. Port Harcourt: M & J Grand Orbit.
sources.note: Morphological comparison; tone marked; no mention of stress.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1981. Syllable weight and tone. Linguistic Inquiry 12(4): 670-673.
sources.note: Kanakuru, Bole and Hausa are all tonal; Kanakuru -ak verbal-noun tone determined by syllable weight (citing Newman 1974); syllable weight 'like stress—which also does not normally cooccur with distinctive tone—is rhythmic (metrical)'. Nothing on stress placement in Kanakuru.

sources.citation: Frajzyngier, Zygmunt. 1976. Rule inversion in Chadic: an explanation. Studies in African Linguistics 7(2): 195-210.
sources.note: Kanakuru plural formation and consonant alternations; no stress/accent statement (the only 'stress' hit in the issue is in another article on downdrift).

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1972. Study Kanakuru, understand Hausa. Harsunan Nijeriya 2: 1-13.
sources.note: Comparative morphology/sound-change notes; no mention of stress or accent.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1972. Syllable weight as a phonological variable. Studies in African Linguistics 3(3): 301-323.
sources.note: Kanakuru section 4.2 (pp. 310-313): light = (c)v, heavy = (c)vc; verb tone predictable from initial-consonant class; -ak verbal nouns Hi-Hi after light, Hi-Lo after heavy first syllable; p. 312 aside about the suffix failing to keep Hi tone 'after a heavy, stressed syllable'. No stress-placement statement.

sources.citation: Schuh, Russell G. 1972. Rule inversion in Chadic. Studies in African Linguistics 3(3): 379-397.
sources.note: Kanakuru intervocalic consonant weakening; a full-text search for stress/accent the whole issue finds no stress/accent statement about Kanakuru.

sources.citation: Newman, Paul. 1970. Historical sound laws in Hausa and in Dera (Kanakuru). Journal of West African Languages 7: 39-51.
sources.note: Consonant sound laws only; 'Tone does not enter into the discussion' (p. 40); no mention of stress. Gives informant/dialect information (Shani, Shellen).

sources.citation: Arnott, David W. 1977. Review of The Kanakuru language. Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 40: 655-656.

sources.note: Short review by a Chadic/Fula specialist; may summarise the phonology chapter.
